title: Contraindications and Adverse Effects
subtitle: Screen, monitor and respond rather than assuming harmlessness
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating contraindications and adverse effects within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain contraindications and adverse effects without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in contraindications and adverse effects.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to contraindications and adverse effects.

sections.explainSimply: Neurofeedback is often tolerated, but some people report headache, fatigue, agitation, sleep change, emotional activation or symptom worsening.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Risk depends on protocol, individual vulnerability, comorbidity and implementation. Seizure risk, acute instability, psychosis, mania, dissociation and medical causes require appropriate assessment.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Use informed consent, conservative dosing, symptom tracking, stop rules and referral pathways. Serious or persistent deterioration requires clinical and medical review.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A medication review: benefit, burden, adverse effects and alternatives must remain visible throughout care.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand contraindications and adverse effects to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.clinicalPearl: Measure benefit and harm with the same seriousness.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using contraindications and adverse effects predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: “Non-invasive” does not mean “cannot cause harm.” Evidence classification: adverse effects documented; incidence uncertain.
